title: The afternoon pause (Berakhot 6b)
hookLine: a few minutes in the working day; the Talmud says to be especially careful with this prayer
carry: pray in the middle of the day

lines: TEN MINUTES IN A CONFERENCE ROOM.
cards: Three-fifteen on a weekday. The inbox is full, a meeting just ran long, the kids need picking up, the coffee's gone cold. Nobody plans anything holy for three-fifteen.
Morning has its own mood, fresh and new. Night has its own, quiet and closing. But the middle of the afternoon is pure busyness.

And that's exactly where Jewish tradition puts one of its three daily prayers. In office buildings in some cities, a small group gathers in a conference room for ten minutes, then goes back to their desks.

teach.b: The afternoon prayer is called Mincha. The word means a gift, or an offering. The Bible uses it for the Temple's afternoon offering, and the prayer took its name from that hour of the day.
It's short: a psalm, the Amidah said silently, and on most weekdays a few closing lines. The Talmud links each daily prayer to one of the ancestors, and gives the afternoon to Isaac.

teach.h: ISAAC IN THE FIELD AT EVENTIDE.
teach.b: In Genesis, in the old Jewish translation, "Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The rabbis read that meditation as prayer: Isaac, alone in a field toward evening, before he even sees Rebekah coming.
Now the line this day is named for.
In tractate Berakhot, page 6b, a teacher says in the name of another: a person should always be especially careful with the afternoon prayer. Why this one? Later commentators give a plain answer.
Morning prayer comes before the day starts, and evening prayer after it ends.
Mincha lands right in the middle, when you're busiest and it's easiest to let it slip. Being careful with it means stepping out of the stream on purpose.
The Talmud gives its own reason too, a story about a prophet on a mountain, and that's tomorrow.

teach.h: PRAY IN THE MIDDLE OF THE DAY.
teach.b: Today, just the shape of it: a gift given in the middle of the day.

how: Mincha is said daily from early afternoon until sunset: Ashrei (Psalm 145), the silent Amidah with its repetition when there is a minyan, and on most weekdays Tachanun and Aleinu. Many people gather for it at work or between errands.

games.q: it's three-fifteen. your day is packed. the Talmud says to be especially careful with which prayer?
games.why: Berakhot 6b: always be careful with Mincha, the one that falls in the middle of the busy day.

practice: Wherever you are in your day, stop what you're doing, sit up straight, close your eyes and breathe out the last hour.
If you pray, this is a moment for it, in any words you have; if not, just stand in the middle of your day like Isaac in his field, and look around.
